payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are both the giraffes and the surrounding environment consistently represented as drawn forms rather than photographic forms beneath a surface effect?
node.criteria: Pass if drawn contours, interior marks and shading represent the principal subjects and the surrounding vegetation, ground and background, so substantial scene regions no longer rely on photographic surface detail or photographic tonal modeling. Inspect the giraffes' bodies and markings as well as the full environment; sketch-like silhouettes alone do not establish this condition. Fail if substantial regions retain photographic rendering beneath added grain, outlined edges or smudging, even when other regions have been convincingly drawn. Background blur or loss of detail alone does not establish drawn representation. Recognizable anatomy, retained composition, accurate markings, fine drawn detail and retained colors are permitted; source resemblance alone is not evidence of photographic rendering. Return unknown only when the images are unavailable or genuinely insufficient to distinguish the rendering, not merely because evidence differs across regions.
node.binding: Compare the input and edited images for the requested transformation into a chalk-made drawing, examining the giraffes' bodies and markings as well as the vegetation, ground and background.

node_traces.evidence: The giraffes have prominent drawn outlines and chalk-like marks, but their bodies and spots still retain much of the source's photographic tonal modeling. The environment is heavily blurred and smeared, yet the vegetation, ground, and background do not consistently read as drawn forms; substantial regions appear to be photographic content softened beneath a grainy surface effect.

The giraffes have prominent drawn outlines and chalk-like marks, but their bodies and spots still retain much of the source's photographic tonal modeling. The environment is heavily blurred and smeared, yet the vegetation, ground, and background do not consistently read as drawn forms; substantial regions appear to be photographic content softened beneath a grainy surface effect.

The edited image renders both giraffes with drawn outlines and repeated interior chalk-like marks, while the vegetation, ground, and background are also broadly re-rendered with soft, streaked shading rather than retaining the source's photographic surface detail. The scene remains recognizable, but substantial regions across both subjects and environment read as drawn forms.

The edited image renders both giraffes with drawn outlines, hatch-like interior markings, and shaded forms. The vegetation, ground, hills, and sky are also broadly re-rendered with soft, directional chalk-like strokes rather than retaining the source's photographic surface detail. Some scene features remain recognizable, but substantial regions across both subjects and environment read as drawn forms.

The edited image represents both giraffes with drawn outlines, hatch-like interior markings, and shaded forms. The vegetation, ground, hills, and sky are also rendered with broad chalky strokes and softened drawn shading rather than retaining the source's photographic surface detail. The composition and recognizable giraffe markings remain, but substantial regions across both subjects and environment have been transformed into drawn forms.

response.content: {"text":"The binding is too vague and its “photographic forms beneath a surface effect” phrasing may bias the decision toward treating chalk texture, blur, or grain as evidence of failure. Keep the comparison anchored to the requested chalk drawing, and make the decision inspect both giraffes and the environment for actual drawn contours, marks, and shading versus retained photographic modeling; texture or smudging alone is not decisive. The traces show a real borderline distinction: the giraffes have drawn outlines and marks, while their bodies retain photographic tonal structure and much of the environment is blurred or smeared rather than clearly re-rendered. Other runs judge broad chalk-like environmental strokes sufficient. Clarify how to weigh these regions against the criterion that substantial scene areas must read as drawn, without letting one convincing region stand in for the whole scene or treating source resemblance as proof of photographic rendering. Preserve the partial-progress distinction: visible chalk-drawing changes count as progress, but do not automatically establish complete fulfillment. All traces are valid observations with no dependency or transport failures; the disagreement is semantic, not missing evidence. Repeated high-confidence variation is a calibration signal, not grounds to force a label."}
